A. A. Milne.bio: A. A. Milne was an English writer who worked for Punch. He wrote the Pooh stories for his son Christopher Robin. He wrote plays and mysteries as well.

Abbie Farwell Brown.bio: Abbie Farwell Brown was an American author of children's books, many drawn from folklore and myth. She was part of the Boston literary scene. She wrote many books of retold stories.

Adèle Geras.bio: British author born in Jerusalem. She taught and wrote in Manchester. She writes many novels.

Alan Garner.bio: Alan Garner is an English novelist whose books draw on myth and landscape. He grew up in a family of craftsmen in Cheshire, which inspired the Stone Book Quartet. He lives in a house near Alderley Edge.

Albert Payson Terhune.bio: Albert Payson Terhune was an American author best known for his stories about collies. He raised the dogs at his estate, Sunnybank, in New Jersey. His books about Lad made him famous.

Alexandre Dumas.bio: Alexandre Dumas was a prolific French novelist and playwright. His father was a general of mixed-race heritage. His adventure novels remain popular.

Alice L. Hopf.bio: Alice Lightner Hopf wrote nonfiction books about animals for children. Further personal details were not verified.

Allan Baillie.bio: Allan Baillie is an Australian author of children's adventure novels. He worked as a journalist and photographer before writing for young people. Adrift was his first novel for children.

Amy Tan.bio: Amy Tan is an American author of The Joy Luck Club.

Ann Nolan Clark.bio: Ann Nolan Clark was an author and educator who worked with Native American and Latin American communities. She wrote books for children in places where she had taught, and won the Newbery Medal in 1953. Many of her books were also published in the languages of the communities she worked with.

Anna Sewell.bio: English author who was largely housebound after an injury. She wrote Black Beauty in her final years. It became a landmark of animal welfare.

Anne Lindbergh.bio: American author, daughter of Charles and Anne Morrow Lindbergh. She wrote children's books. She died young.

Armstrong Sperry.bio: Armstrong Sperry was an author and illustrator who traveled the South Pacific as a young man. He wrote Call It Courage after hearing a Polynesian legend. It won the Newbery Medal in 1941.

Arnold A. Griese.bio: Arnold A. Griese was an American author who wrote about Alaska Native cultures.
known_for: At the Mouth of the Luckiest River

Arthur Bowie Chrisman.bio: American author of folk-tale retellings. He won the first-ever tale Newbery. He farmed in Virginia.

Arthur Conan Doyle.bio: Arthur Conan Doyle was a Scottish physician and writer who created Sherlock Holmes. He based the detective's methods partly on a professor he knew in medical school. He grew tired of Holmes and killed him off, but public pressure brought him back.

Arthur Roth.bio: Arthur Roth wrote adventure novels for young readers. Personal details were not verified.

Astrid Lindgren.bio: Astrid Lindgren was a Swedish author who invented Pippi Longstocking while telling stories to her sick daughter. She was also a strong advocate for children's and animals' rights. Her books are among the most translated in the world.

Avi.bio: Avi (Avi Wortis) is a writer of historical fiction, mysteries and fantasy. A school teacher and librarian before he wrote full-time, he got his start as a writer partly because of his own difficulty with writing as a child. His single name comes from a childhood nickname given by his twin sister.
known_for: The True Confessions of Charlotte Doyle

Barbara Brooks Wallace.bio: American mystery author. She won Edgar Awards. She wrote for children.

Barbara Corcoran.bio: Barbara Corcoran was a teacher and author of young adult novels. She wrote on teens facing life challenges. She lived in Montana.

Barbara Kingsolver.bio: Barbara Kingsolver trained as a biologist and became a novelist. She grew up partly in the Congo. She is known for literary fiction with social themes.

Beatrice Culleton.bio: Culleton Mosionier is a Metis author whose first novel drew on her foster care experience.

Beatrix Potter.bio: Potter was a writer and illustrator who became a conservationist, giving land to the National Trust.

Bernice G. Anderson.bio: Bernice G. Anderson was an author of Native American folk-tale collections. Little biographical information was found.

Betsy Byars.bio: Betsy Byars was an American author of more than sixty books for children. She wrote while her four children were small and often drew on their lives. She was also a licensed pilot.

Betty Sterman.bio: Betty Sterman co-wrote children's books with a spouse or relative. Little biographical information was found.

Beverly Cleary.bio: Beverly Cleary was an American author of children's books. A former librarian, she wrote stories of ordinary children after a boy asked her where the books about kids like him were. She was named a Living Legend by the Library of Congress.

Brian Jacques.bio: Brian Jacques was a British author who worked as a sailor, a bus driver and a milkman before he wrote Redwall. He began the first book for children at a school for the blind, where he delivered milk. He read his stories aloud with great gusto.

Bruce Coville.bio: Bruce Coville has written many fantasy books for children. He worked as a toymaker and a teacher.

C. S. Lewis.bio: Lewis was an Oxford and Cambridge scholar of medieval literature. He wrote the Narnia books for children, partly inspired by children evacuated to his house in WWII. He was a close friend of J. R. R. Tolkien.

Carlo Collodi.bio: Carlo Collodi was the pen name of Carlo Lorenzini, a journalist and political writer. He serialized Pinocchio in a children's newspaper. The pen name came from his mother's home village.

Carol Fenner.bio: Carol Fenner was a children's author and illustrator. She won a Newbery Honor for Yolonda's Genius.

Carol Ryrie Brink.bio: Carol Ryrie Brink was an American author who wrote novels and children's books. Her best-known book was inspired by her grandmother's tales of frontier childhood. She won the Newbery Medal for Caddie Woodlawn.

Caroline Arnold.bio: Caroline Arnold is an author of many nonfiction picture books about animals, dinosaurs and science. She often photographs or visits the places she writes about. She has written over 150 books.
known_for: A Walk on the Great Barrier Reef

Carolyn Sherwin Bailey.bio: Bailey was a teacher and editor who wrote many books for young children. She won the Newbery for Miss Hickory.
Carolyn Sherwin Bailey.birthplace: Hoosick Falls, New York, United States

Carolyn Sloan.bio: Little biographical information found for this author.

Catherine Edwards Sadler.bio: Catherine Edwards Sadler is an author who adapted classic stories, including Sherlock Holmes tales, for young readers. Little biographical detail is readily available.

Charles Dickens.bio: Dickens was the greatest novelist of Victorian England. He worked in a factory as a boy when his father was imprisoned for debt, which shaped his books. His serial novels were immensely popular.

Charles G. Waugh.bio: Charles G. Waugh is an American professor and anthology editor who often worked with Martin Greenberg. Personal details were not verified.

Charlotte Brontë.bio: Charlotte Brontë was the eldest of the famous Brontë sisters, who grew up on the Yorkshire moors. She wrote under the pen name Currer Bell. She published Jane Eyre in 1847, to wide acclaim.

Chris Riddell.bio: Chris Riddell is a British illustrator and political cartoonist, born in South Africa. He was the UK Children's Laureate. He illustrated the Edge Chronicles and wrote and drew many other books.

Clive King.bio: Clive King was a British author. He wrote Stig of the Dump.

Colby Rodowsky.bio: Colby Rodowsky wrote young-adult and children's novels, many set in Baltimore. She began writing while raising her family. Her books explore family relationships.

Cynthia Rylant.bio: Rylant grew up in West Virginia Appalachian towns and worked as a librarian before writing. She has written picture books and novels.

Cynthia Voigt.bio: Voigt was an English teacher who wrote the Tillerman cycle. She won the Newbery for Dicey's Song.

D. J. Enright.bio: D. J. Enright was a poet, novelist and critic who taught in several countries. He wrote a few books for children.

Daniel Defoe.bio: Daniel Defoe was a merchant, journalist and novelist. He wrote Robinson Crusoe near the end of his life. He is often called a father of the English novel.

Deborah Howe.bio: Deborah Howe was an American author who co-wrote Bunnicula with her husband James. She died young.

Dhan Gopal Mukerji.bio: Mukerji moved to the US to study and became a writer. He wrote about India for American children, and was the first Asian-American Newbery winner.

Diana Wynne Jones.bio: Diana Wynne Jones was a British fantasy writer. She grew up in wartime England. She wrote Howl's Moving Castle.

Dick King-Smith.bio: English farmer turned teacher turned children's author. He began writing in his fifties. His books feature farm animals.

Dodie Smith.bio: English novelist and playwright. She wrote 101 Dalmatians. She owned Dalmatians.

Donald J. Sobol.bio: American author of Encyclopedia Brown. He served in WWII. He wrote over 100 books.

Donna Jo Napoli.bio: Donna Jo Napoli is a linguistics professor and children's writer. She retells fairy tales with fresh angles.
known_for: Jimmy, the Pickpocket of the Palace

Doris Gates.bio: Doris Gates was an American librarian and author of children's books. She wrote about California and common people, and her Blue Willow was a Newbery Honor book. She also wrote the Greek myth retellings.

E. B. White.bio: White was a New Yorker essayist and co-author of The Elements of Style. He wrote Charlotte's Web at his farm in Maine, inspired by a spider he watched in his barn.
E. B. White.birthplace: Mount Vernon, New York, United States

E. L. Konigsburg.bio: Konigsburg won two Newbery awards, including for her first book. She trained as a chemist before writing for children and drew on her own family and her daughter's experiences.
known_for: From the Mixed-Up Files of Mrs. Basil E. Frankweiler

E. Nesbit.bio: Edith Nesbit wrote humorous fantasy and realistic stories for children with lively real-feeling kids. She was also a socialist and a founder of the Fabian Society. She wrote many books after her family needed money.
known_for: The Story of the Treasure Seekers

E. W. Hildick.bio: English author of school and adventure stories. He wrote many series. He taught.
known_for: The Dragon That Lived Under Manhattan

Edward Eager.bio: Eager was a playwright and lyricist who began writing children's books for his son, inspired by E. Nesbit.

Edward Fenton.bio: Edward Fenton was an American writer and translator. He wrote adventure novels for young readers.
known_for: The Riddle of the Red Whale

Eileen Dunlop.bio: Eileen Dunlop is a Scottish writer of historical and supernatural fiction for young people. She also wrote about Scottish history. Her novels often involve old houses.

Eleanor Cameron.bio: Eleanor Cameron was a Canadian-American author. She wrote The Wonderful Flight to the Mushroom Planet.
known_for: The Court of the Stone Children
The Wonderful Flight to the Mushroom Planet

Eleanor Coerr.bio: Eleanor Coerr was a Canadian-born American author. She became interested in Sadako's story while working in Japan. She wrote many picture books and chapter books.
known_for: Sadako and the Thousand Paper Cranes

Eleanor Estes.bio: Eleanor Estes was an American children's author and children's librarian whose books draw on her Connecticut childhood. Her Moffat family stories became classics of everyday life. She won the Newbery Medal for Ginger Pye.

Eleanor Farjeon.bio: Eleanor Farjeon was an English poet and storyteller who grew up in a literary family. She wrote hymns and fairy tales. The Eleanor Farjeon Award honors her.
known_for: Martin Pippin in the Apple Orchard

Elizabeth Borton de Treviño.bio: Elizabeth Borton de Treviño was an American author and journalist who married a Mexican man and lived in Monterrey, Mexico. She wrote on Mexican and Spanish themes. Her Newbery winner told the story of Juan de Pareja.

Elizabeth Coatsworth.bio: Elizabeth Coatsworth was a poet and children's author who lived in Maine. She won the Newbery Medal for The Cat Who Went to Heaven. She was married to writer Henry Beston.
known_for: The Cat Who Went to Heaven

Elizabeth Enright.bio: American author and illustrator from an artistic family. She won the Newbery for Thimble Summer. Her Melendy family books are loved classics.

Elizabeth George Speare.bio: Elizabeth George Speare was an American author of historical novels for young people. She spent years researching her subjects in New England history. She won the Newbery Medal twice, for The Witch of Blackbird Pond and The Bronze Bow.

Elizabeth Janet Gray.bio: Elizabeth Janet Gray, later Vining, was a children's author who won the Newbery Medal for Adam of the Road. She later became tutor to Crown Prince Akihito of Japan.

Elizabeth Yates.bio: Elizabeth Yates wrote many children's books and biographies. Her work often drew on New England life. She won the Newbery Medal for Amos Fortune, Free Man.

Ellen Raskin.bio: Ellen Raskin was an American author and illustrator who designed hundreds of book covers, including the first edition of A Wrinkle in Time. Her mysteries mix word games and visual puzzles. She illustrated every book she wrote.
known_for: Nothing Ever Happens on My Block

Emily Brontë.bio: Emily Brontë was an English novelist and poet, the sister of Charlotte and Anne. She wrote under the name Ellis Bell. Wuthering Heights, her only novel, was published a year before her death.

Enid Bagnold.bio: Enid Bagnold was a British novelist and playwright. She served as a nurse in World War I. National Velvet, her best-known novel, was made into a film with Elizabeth Taylor.

Ernest Hemingway.bio: Ernest Hemingway was an American novelist and journalist known for sparse, direct prose. He served as an ambulance driver in World War I and lived in Paris, Cuba and elsewhere. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1954.
known_for: The Old Man and the Sea

Esther Forbes.bio: American novelist and historian. She won the Pulitzer for history. Johnny Tremain won the Newbery.
known_for: Paul Revere and the World He Lived In

Eth Clifford.bio: Eth Clifford was an American author of children's books. She wrote many popular books for young readers, including the Harvey series.
known_for: Help! I'm a Prisoner in the Library

Florence Atwater.bio: Florence Atwater co-wrote Mr. Popper's Penguins with her husband Richard. The story came from a family joke about penguins. She continued to promote the book after his death.

Florence Parry Heide.bio: Florence Parry Heide wrote over a hundred children's books, many of them humorous or darkly funny. She wrote with her daughter and several illustrators. She was best known for The Shrinking of Treehorn.

Frances Hodgson Burnett.bio: Frances Hodgson Burnett was a British-American novelist who emigrated as a teenager to Tennessee. She wrote to support her family and became a famed author of children's classics. She loved gardens and cultivated them at her home on Long Island.

Garrison Keillor.bio: American humorist and radio host. He created A Prairie Home Companion. He wrote Lake Wobegon.

Garry Disher.bio: Garry Disher is an Australian novelist who writes crime fiction and books for younger readers. He grew up on a farm in South Australia. His crime novels include the Wyatt series.

Gary Paulsen.bio: Gary Paulsen was an American author of more than 200 books. He was an Iditarod racer. He wrote Hatchet.

Gene DeWeese.bio: Gene DeWeese was an American author who wrote science fiction and mystery novels, including books for young readers. He also wrote Star Trek novels. Few personal details are recorded.
known_for: The Adventures of a Two-Minute Werewolf

Gene Stratton-Porter.bio: Gene Stratton-Porter was an American author, photographer and naturalist. She wrote popular novels set in Indiana's Limberlost swamp. She later turned to film production.

Gennady Spirin.bio: Russian-born illustrator who moved to the United States. His paintings were inspired by Renaissance masters. He illustrated many fairy tales.

George Selden.bio: George Selden was an American author best known for The Cricket in Times Square. He lived in New York and worked as a writer and playwright. His cricket story was inspired by a real cricket he heard in the Times Square subway.

Gertrude Moderow.bio: No verified information found about this adaptor.

Gian Paolo Ceserani.bio: Italian author and historian. He wrote history for young readers. He collaborated with Ventura.

H. M. Hoover.bio: Helen Mary Hoover wrote science-fiction novels for young readers, often exploring ecology and other worlds. Her books are known for strong young heroines. She was an editor and a writer during her career.

Hans Christian Andersen.bio: Hans Christian Andersen was a Danish author best known for his fairy tales. Born into poverty, he left home as a teenager to pursue a career in Copenhagen's theatre. His stories mix humour, longing and sorrow.

Harold Keith.bio: Harold Keith was an American author and sports information director at the University of Oklahoma. He won the Newbery Medal for Rifles for Watie.

Harper Lee.bio: Lee wrote To Kill a Mockingbird, drawing on her Alabama childhood. She was a friend of Truman Capote.

Harriet Beecher Stowe.bio: American author and abolitionist. Her novel galvanized opposition to slavery. She came from a famous preaching family.

Helen Cresswell.bio: Helen Cresswell was an English author and television writer. She wrote more than a hundred books and adapted many for TV. She is known for Lizzie Dripping and The Bagthorpe Saga.

Hilda van Stockum.bio: Dutch-born author and painter who grew up in Ireland. She lived through wartime Europe. She wrote of family life.

Honoré Morrow.bio: Morrow wrote historical novels and biographies.

Howard Pyle.bio: Pyle was an illustrator and author who shaped the look of pirates and knights, and taught N. C. Wyeth.
known_for: The Merry Adventures of Robin Hood
The Story of King Arthur and His Knights

Hugh Lofting.bio: Hugh Lofting was a British-born engineer who created Doctor Dolittle in letters he wrote to his children from the trenches of World War I. He thought the horrors of war made it hard to write about the injured horses, so he invented an animal doctor instead. He later settled in California.

Humphrey Harman.bio: Humphrey Harman wrote on Africa and told African tales. Little verified biographical information is available.

Isaac Bashevis Singer.bio: Isaac Bashevis Singer wrote in Yiddish and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1978. He grew up in a Warsaw rabbi's household and later moved to New York. He began writing for children late in life, with help from his translators.
known_for: Zlateh the Goat and Other Stories

J. K. Rowling.bio: J. K. Rowling conceived the idea for Harry Potter on a delayed train. She wrote the first book as a single mother. The series became the best-selling book series in history.
known_for: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone

J. M. Barrie.bio: Barrie wrote plays and novels, and Peter Pan emerged from stories he told the Llewelyn Davies boys. He gave the rights to Great Ormond Street Hospital.

J. R. R. Tolkien.bio: J. R. R. Tolkien was a philologist and Oxford professor who created Middle-earth. He began writing The Hobbit as a bedtime story for his children. He fought in World War I and shaped modern fantasy.

Jack London.bio: Jack London was an American novelist and journalist. After working jobs from oyster pirate to Klondike gold prospector, he turned to writing about life on the edge. He became one of the first writers to earn a fortune from fiction.

Jacqueline Balcells.bio: Jacqueline Balcells was a Chilean-born children's author.

James Baldwin.bio: American educator and author of children's retellings. He wrote legends. He worked as a publisher's editor.

James Houston.bio: James Houston was a Canadian author, artist and Arctic explorer who lived for years among the Inuit. He introduced Inuit art to the wider world and wrote novels shaped by what he learned. He later lived in Connecticut.

James Howe.bio: James Howe is an American author who wrote the Bunnicula series. His books range from humor to serious issues.

Jan Slepian.bio: Jan Slepian is an American author of children's books. She worked with her friend Ann Seidler on several works. She wrote The Alfred Summer.

Jane Goodall.bio: Jane Goodall was a primatologist who studied wild chimpanzees at Gombe. She started with no formal training. She became a leading conservation advocate.

Jane Langton.bio: Jane Langton wrote fantasies and mysteries set in Concord, Massachusetts. She illustrated some of her own books. She won a Newbery Honor.

Jane Leslie Conly.bio: Jane Leslie Conly is a children's author and daughter of Robert C. O'Brien. She wrote sequels to her father's work after his death. She also wrote her own novels.
known_for: Racso and the Rats of NIMH
Rasco and the Rats of NIMH

Jane Yolen.bio: Jane Yolen is a prolific American author of children's books, fantasy and poetry. She has written well over three hundred books. She has been called the Hans Christian Andersen of America.

Janet Hickman.bio: Janet Hickman is an American children's author and former teacher. She wrote novels and short stories for young readers. Further details were not verified.

Janet Taylor Lisle.bio: American author of children's novels. She won a Newbery Honor. She lives in Rhode Island.

Jay Williams.bio: Jay Williams was an American author of books for children and adults, including historical novels. He teamed with Raymond Abrashkin for the Danny Dunn series. He also wrote fantasy and fairy tale picture books.
known_for: Danny Dunn and the Anti-Gravity Paint

Jean Craighead George.bio: Jean Craighead George was a naturalist and author who wrote nature stories for children. She grew up in a family of naturalists, and kept pets of every kind including owls and weasels. Her books, such as My Side of the Mountain, came from long experience of wild places.

Jean Fritz.bio: Jean Fritz was born in China to missionary parents and moved to the US as a teen. She wrote lively, well-researched histories and biographies for children.
known_for: And Then What Happened, Paul Revere?

Jean Merrill.bio: Merrill wrote children's books and worked in publishing. The Pushcart War is her best-known work.

Jerry Spinelli.bio: Spinelli wrote for adults at first, then turned to young readers while raising his children. He won the Newbery Medal for Maniac Magee.

Jill Paton Walsh.bio: Walsh was an English novelist who wrote for children and adults and finished Dorothy Sayers's Lord Peter novels. She was made a Fellow of the Royal Society of Literature.

Jim Kjelgaard.bio: American author of outdoor and dog stories. He worked as a trapper and guide. He wrote dozens of books for young readers.

Joan Aiken.bio: Joan Aiken was a prolific English author of children's and adult fiction, best known for the Wolves Chronicles. She grew up in a literary household as the daughter of poet Conrad Aiken and began writing stories young. She wrote her first Wolves book as a bedtime story for her own child.

Joan Kahn.bio: Kahn was an editor of mystery fiction and anthologies.

Joan W. Blos.bio: American author who also taught. She won the Newbery. She wrote history.

Johanna Spyri.bio: Swiss author whose Heidi has been loved worldwide. She turned to writing in middle age. She drew on Alpine life.

John D. Fitzgerald.bio: Fitzgerald based the Great Brain books on his own boyhood in Utah. He wrote them as a way to tell the stories of his childhood and his clever older brother.

John Steinbeck.bio: American novelist who chronicled California life. He won the Nobel Prize in 1962. He wrote while working odd jobs and was fascinated by marine biology.

Jon Scieszka.bio: Jon Scieszka is a former teacher who writes funny books for kids. He was the first National Ambassador for Young People's Literature and founded the Guys Read project. He is the author of The Stinky Cheese Man.
known_for: The True Story of the 3 Little Pigs

Jonathan Swift.bio: Jonathan Swift was an Anglo-Irish satirist and clergyman who became dean of St. Patrick's Cathedral in Dublin. He wrote Gulliver's Travels as a biting satire. He also wrote A Modest Proposal.

Joseph Krumgold.bio: Krumgold was a filmmaker who turned to children's novels. He won two Newbery Medals, the first author to do so.
Joseph Krumgold.birthplace: Jersey City, New Jersey, United States

Josephine Poole.bio: Josephine Poole was a British author of children's and young-adult books, many with a touch of the supernatural. She also wrote adult novels. Few personal details were verified.

Judith Kerr.bio: British author and illustrator who fled Nazi Germany as a child. She wrote about her flight. She also created The Tiger Who Came to Tea.
known_for: The Tiger Who Came to Tea

Judy Blume.bio: Blume began writing while raising her kids. She is known for honest books on growing up and her Fudge stories.
known_for: Tales of a Fourth Grade Nothing
Are You There God? It's Me, Margaret

Jules Verne.bio: Verne is a pioneer of science fiction, whose adventure novels have been translated widely.
known_for: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea
Around the World in Eighty Days

Karen Cushman.bio: Karen Cushman was inspired by her studies of medieval history. She wrote historical fiction about girls. She won the Newbery Medal for The Midwife's Apprentice.

Kate Seredy.bio: Seredy was an illustrator who emigrated to the US in 1922. She drew on her childhood in Hungary for her books and illustrated them herself.

Katherine Paterson.bio: American writer born to missionary parents in China. She has won the Newbery twice. She wrote Bridge to Terabithia from her son's grief.

Kathryn Lasky.bio: American author of fiction and nonfiction. She wrote Guardians of Ga'Hoole. She writes history too.

Kenneth Grahame.bio: Scottish writer who worked at the Bank of England. He wrote The Wind in the Willows from bedtime stories for his son. He retired early.

L. Frank Baum.bio: L. Frank Baum was an American author who created the Land of Oz. Before writing, he worked as an actor, shopkeeper and journalist. He wrote fourteen Oz novels.

Laura Adams Armer.bio: Armer was a photographer who lived among the Navajo and then wrote about them. She won the Newbery for Waterless Mountain.

Laura Ingalls Wilder.bio: Laura Ingalls Wilder grew up on the American frontier and became a teacher. In her sixties she wrote her childhood memories as the Little House books. Her daughter Rose helped edit them.
known_for: Little House in the Big Woods

Lemony Snicket.bio: Lemony Snicket is the pen name of Daniel Handler.

Leonard Everett Fisher.bio: Leonard Everett Fisher is an American author and illustrator of more than 250 books. He taught at Yale and received many awards.

Leonie Kooiker.bio: Leonie Kooiker is a Dutch children's author. Little verified information is available.

Lewis Carroll.bio: Pen name of Charles Dodgson, mathematician and photographer at Oxford. He told Alice stories on a boat trip. He also wrote nonsense poetry.

Linda Sue Park.bio: Korean-American author. She won the Newbery. She was a journalist first.

Lloyd Alexander.bio: Lloyd Alexander was an American author of fantasy. Stationed in Wales during World War II, he fell in love with Welsh legends, which inspired the Prydain books. He worked as a cartoonist and translator and said he came to writing for children late.
known_for: The Cat Who Wished to Be a Man

Lois Lenski.bio: Lois Lenski was an author and illustrator who wrote regional stories. She visited the places she wrote about to get the details right. She won the Newbery Medal for Strawberry Girl.

Lois Lowry.bio: Lois Lowry grew up in a military family and lived in many places. She is known for writing both humorous and serious children's books. She has won two Newbery Medals.

Louisa May Alcott.bio: Louisa May Alcott grew up in a family of philosophers and reformers in Massachusetts. She worked as a nurse in the Civil War and began writing to help support her family. Little Women was based largely on her own sisters.

Louise Fitzhugh.bio: Louise Fitzhugh was an American writer and illustrator. She grew up in Memphis and moved to New York as an adult. Harriet the Spy was her first and most famous book.
known_for: Nobody's Family Is Going to Change

Lynne Reid Banks.bio: British author who first worked as an actress and journalist. She spent years on an Israeli kibbutz. She wrote the Indian in the Cupboard for her sons.

M. M. Kaye.bio: M. M. Kaye grew up in India. She wrote historical novels, including The Far Pavilions, and children's books.

Mabel Leigh Hunt.bio: Mabel Leigh Hunt was an American children's author with Quaker roots. She wrote historical fiction. She won a Newbery Honor for Better Known as Johnny Appleseed.

Madeleine L'Engle.bio: American author of fantasy, science fiction and memoirs. A Wrinkle in Time was rejected by many publishers before success. She served as librarian at a New York cathedral.

Maia Wojciechowska.bio: Maia Wojciechowska was born in Poland and came to the United States as a young woman. She wrote young-adult novels, and Shadow of a Bull won the Newbery Medal. She also wrote about bullfighting and Spain.

Margaret Mahy.bio: Margaret Mahy was a New Zealand librarian who became a celebrated children's writer. She won the Carnegie Medal twice and the Hans Christian Andersen Award. She was known for flamboyant costumes.

Margot Benary-Isbert.bio: Margot Benary-Isbert was a German-American author who emigrated after World War II. She wrote about postwar family life in Germany.

Marguerite Henry.bio: Marguerite Henry wrote more than fifty books, mostly about horses and other animals. She spent years researching her subjects and often traveled to meet them. She won the Newbery Medal for King of the Wind and is also known for Misty of Chincoteague.

Marguerite de Angeli.bio: De Angeli wrote and illustrated more than 30 books, often about families and history. She won the Newbery Medal for The Door in the Wall.

Maria D. Wilkes.bio: Maria D. Wilkes is an American author.

Maria Gripe.bio: Gripe was a Swedish author of children's novels and won the Hans Christian Andersen Award in 1974.

Marilyn Sachs.bio: American author of realistic children's books. She was a librarian. She wrote about Bronx life.

Marilyn Singer.bio: Marilyn Singer is a prolific author who writes picture books, novels and poetry for children. She grew up in the Bronx. She is known for playful poems.

Marion Dane Bauer.bio: Marion Dane Bauer is an American author of children's and young adult books. She wrote On My Honor.

Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings.bio: American author who moved to rural Florida. She won the Pulitzer Prize. She wrote of the Florida scrub.

Mark Helprin.bio: Mark Helprin is a novelist and journalist, known for his lyrical fiction. He served in the British merchant navy and the Israeli army. He has also written children's books with Chris Van Allsburg.
known_for: A Soldier of the Great War

Mark Twain.bio: Mark Twain was the pen name of Samuel Clemens, a writer and humorist who grew up in Hannibal, Missouri. He worked as a riverboat pilot, and his pen name comes from a river depth call. He became famous across America as a lecturer and storyteller.

Martin H. Greenberg.bio: Martin H. Greenberg was a prolific anthology editor, especially of science fiction and fantasy. He edited or co-edited well over a thousand anthologies. He worked as a university professor before founding a publishing company.

Mary Stolz.bio: Mary Stolz wrote more than 60 books for children and teens. She was a Newbery Honor recipient.

Meindert DeJong.bio: Meindert DeJong was born in a small Friesian village and emigrated to the United States as a child. He wrote warm, humane stories for children, often about animals and Dutch village life. He won the Newbery Medal and the Hans Christian Andersen Award.

Michael Bond.bio: Michael Bond worked as a BBC cameraman before creating Paddington. He saw a lonely toy bear on a shelf on Christmas Eve 1956 and was inspired. The books became beloved worldwide.

Michael Crichton.bio: Michael Crichton was an American author and filmmaker. He trained as a doctor. He created ER.

Michael Dorris.bio: Dorris was a writer and anthropologist of Modoc descent.
known_for: A Yellow Raft in Blue Water

Michael Ende.bio: Ende was a German author whose fantasy novels were widely translated.

Michael Morpurgo.bio: Michael Morpurgo is a British author and former Children's Laureate. He wrote War Horse. He founded Farms for City Children.

Mildred Ames.bio: Mildred Ames wrote young-adult novels, often with a science-fiction angle. Personal details were not verified.
known_for: Without Hats, Who Can Tell the Good Guys

Myron Levoy.bio: American author and teacher. He wrote Alan and Naomi. He taught.

Nancy Bond.bio: Nancy Bond is an American writer of children's fantasy. She lived in England for years and drew on her time in Wales. Her Welsh time-slip novel won a Newbery Honor.

Natalie Babbitt.bio: Natalie Babbitt was an American author and illustrator best known for Tuck Everlasting. She illustrated her own books and her husband's. She often explored big questions about life and death in gentle fantasy.

Nathaniel Benchley.bio: Benchley, son of humorist Robert Benchley and father of Peter Benchley, wrote novels and children's books.
known_for: Only Earth and Sky Last Forever

Nina Bawden.bio: Nina Bawden wrote both novels for adults and children. She was evacuated during WWII, an experience that shaped her fiction. She was shortlisted for the Booker Prize.

Norma Fox Mazer.bio: Norma Fox Mazer was an American author of young-adult novels. She wrote with her husband, Harry Mazer, and often explored family and growing up. She grew up in Glens Falls, New York.
known_for: Mrs. Fish, Ape, and Me, the Dump Queen

Norton Juster.bio: Norton Juster was an American author and architect. He started The Phantom Tollbooth while avoiding work on another project and became a lifelong friend of illustrator Jules Feiffer, who lived upstairs. The book has delighted readers since 1961.

Oliver Butterworth.bio: Oliver Butterworth was an American author and teacher. He wrote humorous children's books.

P. L. Travers.bio: P. L. Travers was born Helen Lyndon Goff and worked as a dancer and actress. She created Mary Poppins while living in England. She had a rocky relationship with Disney's film.

Patricia A. McKillip.bio: American fantasy author. She won the World Fantasy Award. She wrote lyrical fantasy.

Patricia Beatty.bio: Beatty wrote historical novels for young readers set mainly in the American West. She wrote many books, sometimes with her husband.

Patricia C. McKissack.bio: Patricia McKissack wrote many books on African American history and folklore. She and her husband Fredrick wrote together. She won a Newbery Honor.

Patricia Clapp.bio: American historical novelist. She wrote Constance. She lived long.

Patricia MacLachlan.bio: Patricia MacLachlan was an American author who taught English before turning to writing. Her spare novels often explore family and love. She said Sarah, Plain and Tall was inspired by a story told in her own family.

Patricia Reilly Giff.bio: American author and former teacher. She has written many books. She is known for Lily's Crossing.

Paul Creswick.bio: Paul Creswick was an English author known for his retelling of Robin Hood, later illustrated by N. C. Wyeth. Few biographical details could be verified.

Paul Jennings.bio: Paul Jennings is an Australian author known for funny, gross and surprising short stories. He grew up in Australia. His stories are popular with reluctant readers.

Paul Stewart.bio: Paul Stewart is a British author who has written many books for children and teens. He co-created the Edge Chronicles with illustrator Chris Riddell. Their collaboration spans many books.

Paula Fox.bio: Paula Fox was a novelist and children's author who won the Newbery Medal and the Hans Christian Andersen Award. She had a difficult, unsettled childhood, spending years being passed between caretakers. Her adult novel Desperate Characters was revived late in her life.

Pearl S. Buck.bio: Buck grew up in China as the daughter of missionaries. She won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1938.

Penelope Farmer.bio: Penelope Farmer is an English author known for children's fantasy. Her novels, including Charlotte Sometimes, are known for being thoughtful.

Peter Zachary Cohen.bio: Peter Zachary Cohen was an American writer of children's fiction and plays. He taught English at Kansas State University. His books include Foal Creek and Calm Horse, Wild Night.

Philippa Pearce.bio: Pearce grew up in a mill house in Cambridgeshire, which inspired Tom's Midnight Garden. She worked as a BBC scriptwriter and editor before writing.

Phyllis A. Whitney.bio: Phyllis A. Whitney was an American author of mysteries for young people and adults. She spent her childhood in Asia and wrote many books about girls solving mysteries. She kept writing into her nineties.
known_for: The Mystery of the Haunted Pool

Phyllis Reynolds Naylor.bio: Phyllis Reynolds Naylor wrote over 140 books. She won the Newbery Medal for Shiloh. She started writing as a child.

Piero Ventura.bio: Italian illustrator known for historical picture books. He collaborated often. He is best known for Venice and others.

R. J. Unstead.bio: R. J. Unstead was a British teacher and author of many popular history books for children. His books helped make history easy to read for schools.

Rachel Field.bio: Rachel Field was a poet, novelist and playwright. She won the Newbery Medal for Hitty. She died young at age 47.

Ralph Moody.bio: Ralph Moody was a rancher, cowboy and storyteller who wrote about his boyhood in Colorado. He wrote his first book at the urging of an editor, in his fifties. His books follow his Little Britches years.

Randall Jarrell.bio: Randall Jarrell was an American poet, critic and novelist who also wrote for children. He taught at the University of North Carolina at Greensboro. His children's books were illustrated by Maurice Sendak.

Raymond Abrashkin.bio: Raymond Abrashkin was an American educator and author who co-created the Danny Dunn series with Jay Williams. He taught in a New York school. He died in 1960 while the series was just beginning.
known_for: Danny Dunn and the Anti-Gravity Paint

Richard Adams.bio: Richard Adams worked as a civil servant before publishing Watership Down. He first told the story to his daughters on a car journey. It became a huge success.

Richard Atwater.bio: Richard Atwater was a newspaper columnist and teacher of Greek. He wrote Mr. Popper's Penguins with his wife Florence late in his life. The book was an immediate success.

Roald Dahl.bio: Roald Dahl was a bestselling children's author who also worked as a fighter pilot and a spy during World War II. He began writing for children after telling bedtime stories to his own kids. He kept a writing hut in his garden and wrote with a clipboard on his lap.

Robert C. O'Brien.bio: Robert C. O'Brien was the pen name of Robert Leslie Conly, an editor at National Geographic. He wrote Mrs. Frisby and the Rats of NIMH, which won the Newbery Medal. He died before finishing his last book, which his family completed.
known_for: Mrs. Frisby and the Rats of NIMH

Robert Lawson.bio: Robert Lawson was an American author and illustrator. He illustrated The Story of Ferdinand and wrote and illustrated his own books. He won both the Caldecott and Newbery Medals.

Robert Louis Stevenson.bio: Robert Louis Stevenson was a Scottish novelist and travel writer who suffered from poor health all his life. He wrote Treasure Island for his stepson. He spent his last years in Samoa.
known_for: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde

Robert McCloskey.bio: Robert McCloskey was an American author and illustrator known for his careful drawings. He won the Caldecott Medal twice. He studied animals closely, even keeping ducks in his apartment to sketch.

Robert Newman.bio: Robert Newman was an American author best known for children's mysteries. He wrote detective stories in a series. Few biographical details could be verified.
known_for: The Case of the Baker Street Irregular
The Case of the Vanishing Corpse

Robert Siegel.bio: Robert Siegel is a poet and novelist who taught writing at a university in Wisconsin. He is best known for the Whalesong trilogy. He also wrote poems for adults.

Robin McKinley.bio: Robin McKinley writes fantasy that often retells fairy tales. She grew up as the daughter of a naval officer and moved often, which made books her constant companion. She also writes about dogs and horses and has lived in England.

Roger Lea MacBride.bio: American lawyer, politician and writer. He was Laura Ingalls Wilder's daughter's heir. He wrote the Rocky Ridge series.

Rose Wilder Lane.bio: Lane was a journalist and the daughter of Laura Ingalls Wilder, whom she helped edit.
Rose Wilder Lane.birthplace: De Smet, Dakota Territory, United States

Rosemary Sutcliff.bio: Rosemary Sutcliff was a British author of historical fiction for young readers. She used a wheelchair for much of her life, due to illness as a child. Her Roman Britain novels remain classics.

Rosemary Wells.bio: American author and illustrator. She created Max and Ruby. She wrote many books.

Rudyard Kipling.bio: Rudyard Kipling was an English writer born in India. He wrote The Jungle Book and Kim. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1907.

Rumer Godden.bio: Rumer Godden was a British author who spent much of her youth in India. She wrote novels for adults and children, many of which were made into films. Her doll stories are especially loved.

Ruth Manning-Sanders.bio: Ruth Manning-Sanders was a poet and writer who joined a travelling circus as a young woman. In her seventies she began a long series of folk-tale collections, such as A Book of Dragons. She lived in Cornwall.

Ruth Sawyer.bio: Sawyer was a storyteller who collected folk tales and won the Newbery for Roller Skates.

Ruth Stiles Gannett.bio: Gannett wrote My Father's Dragon at age 22 based on stories she heard from her father.

Samuel Sterman.bio: Samuel Sterman co-wrote children's books with a spouse or relative. Little biographical information was found.

Scott O'Dell.bio: O'Dell wrote historical novels after a career as a screenwriter and journalist. He won the Newbery for Island of the Blue Dolphins and set up an award for historical fiction.

Sheila Burnford.bio: Sheila Burnford was born in Scotland and moved to Canada, where she lived in northern Ontario. She wrote The Incredible Journey after her family's pets inspired her. It became a worldwide success.

Sheila Garrigue.bio: Sheila Garrigue is an American author who wrote about children's lives during the war. She was inspired by true evacuee stories.
known_for: All the Children Were Sent Away
The Eternal Spring of Mr. Ito

Shel Silverstein.bio: Shel Silverstein was an American poet, songwriter and cartoonist. He wrote and illustrated books such as Where the Sidewalk Ends. He also wrote songs such as A Boy Named Sue.

Sid Fleischman.bio: Sid Fleischman began his career as a professional magician and later became a novelist and screenwriter. His comic adventure stories often featured tricks and tall tales. He won the Newbery Medal for The Whipping Boy.

Sonia Levitin.bio: Sonia Levitin was born in Berlin and fled with her family from Nazi Germany as a child. She wrote young-adult and children's books, many drawing on her family's immigrant experience. She went on to write dozens of books.

Stephen Crane.bio: Crane was a journalist and novelist who wrote The Red Badge of Courage without having seen battle. He died young.

Sterling North.bio: Sterling North was a writer, literary editor and author of many books. His best-known work, Rascal, is a memoir of a childhood with a pet raccoon in Wisconsin. He also wrote about rural boyhood.

Susan Cooper.bio: Susan Cooper is a British-born writer who worked as a journalist at the Sunday Times and later lived in the United States. She wrote The Dark Is Rising sequence, drawing on Welsh and English legend. She also co-wrote the film Dreamchild.

Susan Dickinson.bio: Susan Dickinson compiled ghost stories for young readers. Little biographical information found.

Suzanne Fisher Staples.bio: Suzanne Fisher Staples is an American author and former journalist. She lived in Pakistan, which inspired Shabanu.

Sylvia Waugh.bio: Sylvia Waugh is a British author who was a teacher before writing. The Mennyms was published when she was in her late fifties. It became a series of five books.

Terry Trueman.bio: Terry Trueman writes young-adult novels about difficult teenage experiences. Stuck in Neutral earned a Printz Honor. He lives in Washington State.

Theodora Du Bois.bio: Theodora Du Bois was an American author of mystery novels and children's books.

Tove Jansson.bio: Tove Jansson was a Finnish-Swedish artist and writer who created the Moomins. She won the Hans Christian Andersen Medal in 1966. She spent summers on a tiny island.

Upton Sinclair.bio: Upton Sinclair was a muckraking novelist and political activist. He wrote The Jungle to expose conditions in the meatpacking industry. He ran for governor of California in 1934.

Uri Orlev.bio: Uri Orlev was an Israeli writer who survived the Warsaw ghetto and Bergen-Belsen as a child. He later moved to Israel and wrote for children in Hebrew. He won the Hans Christian Andersen Award.
known_for: The Man from the Other Side

Ursula K. Le Guin.bio: Ursula K. Le Guin was an American author of fantasy and science fiction. She wrote the Earthsea books. She won many awards.

Virginia Driving Hawk Sneve.bio: Virginia Driving Hawk Sneve was a Lakota author who wrote books for children about Native American life and history. She was a teacher and a member of the Rosebud Sioux Tribe. She was named South Dakota's poet laureate.

Virginia Hamilton.bio: American author who wrote about African American life and folklore. She won the Newbery Medal. She was the first African American to receive it.

Virginia Sorensen.bio: Virginia Sorensen was an American novelist who wrote for adults and children. She grew up in Utah and later lived in Denmark. She won the Newbery Medal for Miracles on Maple Hill.

Walt Morey.bio: Walt Morey was an American author of outdoor stories. He lived in Oregon and Alaska. He is best known for Gentle Ben.

Walter D. Edmonds.bio: American author known for Mohawk Valley historical fiction. He wrote adult and children's books. He won a Newbery Medal.

Walter Farley.bio: Farley wrote The Black Stallion while a student at Columbia University. It became the first of a long series.

Washington Irving.bio: Washington Irving was an early American author and diplomat. He wrote The Legend of Sleepy Hollow and Rip Van Winkle. He was among the first American writers to earn an international reputation.

Will James.bio: Cowboy artist and writer who reinvented himself as a Montana cowboy. He won the Newbery. His real origins were Quebec.

William H. Armstrong.bio: Armstrong was a teacher and farmer. He wrote Sounder, which won the Newbery Medal.

William Mayne.bio: English author of children's fiction rooted in Yorkshire. He won the Carnegie Medal. He was a choirboy at Canterbury Cathedral.

William Pène du Bois.bio: William Pène du Bois was an American author and illustrator who grew up partly in France. He drew from a fascination with inventions and unusual machines. He won the Newbery Medal for The Twenty-One Balloons.

William Steig.bio: American cartoonist and children's author. He began children's books in his sixties. He drew for The New Yorker for decades.

William Stevenson.bio: William Stevenson was a Canadian journalist and author. He wrote A Man Called Intrepid and The Bushbabies.

Willo Davis Roberts.bio: Willo Davis Roberts wrote suspense and mysteries for young readers and adults. She published over a hundred books. She won several awards.
known_for: The Girl with the Silver Eyes

Wilson Rawls.bio: American author raised in the Ozarks. He burned early manuscripts before rewriting. He wrote Where the Red Fern Grows.

Yoshiko Uchida.bio: Uchida was interned with her family during WWII, an experience that shaped her writing about Japanese Americans.

Zilpha Keatley Snyder.bio: American children's author who taught school before writing. She won three Newbery Honors. Her books often draw on childhood in California.

a-bear-called-paddington.summary: The Brown family finds a bear from darkest Peru at Paddington Station, and bring him home. His good manners and mishaps lead to funny chaos.
a-bear-called-paddington.title: A Bear Called Paddington

a-book-of-dragons.summary: A collection of dragon tales from around the world, retold in lively language. It includes stories of heroes, princesses and clever tricksters.
a-book-of-dragons.title: A Book of Dragons

a-brand-new-uncle.note: May be Kate Seredy's 1941 'Listening' or a related title; verify. Likely 'A Brand-New Uncle' published 1961.
a-brand-new-uncle.summary: A sequel to the Hungarian ranch stories in which Kate and Jancsi's world is changed by a new family arrival and village adventure.
a-brand-new-uncle.title: A Brand-New Uncle

a-chance-wild-apple.summary: Details of this book could not be verified.
a-chance-wild-apple.title: A Chance Wild Apple

a-christmas-carol.summary: Miserly Ebenezer Scrooge is visited by his dead partner and three spirits on Christmas Eve. They show him the cost of his coldness and the warmth he has missed.
a-christmas-carol.title: A Christmas Carol

a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur-s-co.summary: A 19th-century American mechanic is knocked out and wakes up in the age of King Arthur. He tries to bring modern ideas to Camelot, with funny and darker consequences.
a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur-s-co.title: A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court

a-foot-in-the-grave.note: Publication year from memory; not verified.
a-foot-in-the-grave.summary: A collection of short tales ranging from spooky to whimsical, with ghosts, odd bargains and surprising twists.
a-foot-in-the-grave.title: A Foot in the Grave

a-gathering-of-days.summary: A New Hampshire girl keeps a journal over a year, recording daily life and a family change.
a-gathering-of-days.title: A Gathering of Days

a-girl-of-the-limberlost.summary: Elnora Comstock grows up in a hard family near the Limberlost swamp in Indiana. She earns her way to school by collecting moths and discovers the beauty of nature.
a-girl-of-the-limberlost.title: A Girl of the Limberlost

a-grass-rope.summary: In a Yorkshire village, children seek a unicorn that legend says only a maiden can lure. A hunt for treasure follows.
a-grass-rope.title: A Grass Rope

a-kingdom-in-a-horse.summary: A boy tries to help a stolen horse make his way. The story focuses on loyalty and freedom.
a-kingdom-in-a-horse.title: A Kingdom in a Horse

a-little-princess.summary: Sara Crewe, a rich and imaginative schoolgirl, is reduced to servitude when her father dies. She keeps her dignity through stories and kindness.
a-little-princess.title: A Little Princess

a-long-vacation.note: Original French title Deux ans de vacances (1888); also published as Two Years' Vacation.
a-long-vacation.summary: A group of schoolboys are carried away on a yacht and wrecked on an uninhabited island. They organize and survive, but tensions arise.
a-long-vacation.title: A Long Vacation

a-newbery-halloween.summary: An anthology of Halloween stories by Newbery-winning authors. It collects spooky and funny tales.
a-newbery-halloween.title: A Newbery Halloween

a-series-of-unfortunate-events-the-bad-b.summary: The three Baudelaire orphans are placed with the villainous Count Olaf. A darkly comic tale.
a-series-of-unfortunate-events-the-bad-b.title: The Bad Beginning

a-single-shard.summary: Orphan Tree-ear dreams of becoming a potter in 12th-century Korea.
a-single-shard.title: A Single Shard

a-string-in-the-harp.summary: After their mother's death, the Jones family moves to Wales where Peter, twelve, finds an ancient harp tuning key that takes him back to the time of the bard Taliesin.
a-string-in-the-harp.title: A String in the Harp

a-swiftly-tilting-planet.setting: Time travel across New England and Wales
a-swiftly-tilting-planet.summary: Charles Wallace, riding a unicorn, travels through time to prevent a world-ending catastrophe. He must change events in the past.
a-swiftly-tilting-planet.title: A Swiftly Tilting Planet

a-tale-of-two-cities.summary: Set in London and Paris during the French Revolution, the novel follows a physician freed from prison, his daughter, and two men whose fates cross. It is about sacrifice, resurrection and the price of revolution.
a-tale-of-two-cities.title: A Tale of Two Cities

a-tale-of-two-cities-adapted-by-patricia.note: Adapted edition; adapter name could not be verified online. Original 1859.
a-tale-of-two-cities-adapted-by-patricia.summary: A simplified retelling of Dickens's story of London and Paris before and during the French Revolution. A family and two men who look alike are swept up in danger.
a-tale-of-two-cities-adapted-by-patricia.title: A Tale of Two Cities

a-trick-of-light.note: Plot from memory; unverified, keep summary vague.
a-trick-of-light.summary: A girl copes with a family move and puzzling events. A young reader mystery with an emotional core.
a-trick-of-light.title: A Trick of Light

a-whisper-in-the-night.summary: A collection of spooky and suspenseful tales that blend the eerie with Aiken's dry humor. Ideal for read-aloud on a dark evening.
a-whisper-in-the-night.title: A Whisper in the Night: Tales of Terror and Suspense

a-wind-in-the-door.setting: Murry home and the inner world of a cell
a-wind-in-the-door.summary: Charles Wallace is ill, and Meg must journey inside his body at the tiniest scale. Some surprising helpers aid her.
a-wind-in-the-door.title: A Wind in the Door

a-wrinkle-in-time.setting: Earth and other planets, mid-20th century
a-wrinkle-in-time.summary: Meg Murry and her brother set out across the universe to find her missing father. Three odd guides help in the fight against a dark force.
a-wrinkle-in-time.title: A Wrinkle in Time

abel-s-island.summary: A pampered mouse is swept away by a storm and trapped on a river island. He learns resourcefulness over a year.
abel-s-island.title: Abel's Island

adam-of-the-road.summary: Adam, an eleven-year-old minstrel's son, is separated from his father and dog in 13th-century England and searches the roads to find them.
adam-of-the-road.title: Adam of the Road

adrift.summary: Flynn and his sister Sally are carried out to sea on a makeshift raft in a story of survival at sea.
adrift.title: Adrift

characters: The Duke and the King — scheming con men
adventures-of-huckleberry-finn.note: Contains racial slurs and portrayals; best read with discussion.
adventures-of-huckleberry-finn.summary: Huck runs away from his violent father and travels down the Mississippi River on a raft with Jim, who has escaped slavery. Along the way they meet tricksters and have to face the cruelties of their world.
adventures-of-huckleberry-finn.title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn

afternoon-of-the-elves.summary: Hillary visits a strange girl's backyard and glimpses a tiny elf village.
afternoon-of-the-elves.title: Afternoon of the Elves

albert-and-victoria.note: Could not verify the book or author through search; details unknown.
albert-and-victoria.summary: A story about Queen Victoria and Prince Albert.
albert-and-victoria.title: Albert and Victoria

alice-s-adventures-in-wonderland.summary: Alice follows a White Rabbit down a hole into a world of nonsense and strange characters.
alice-s-adventures-in-wonderland.title: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland

all-the-children-were-sent-away.summary: British children are evacuated from London to Canada during World War II. They adjust to a new life far from home.
all-the-children-were-sent-away.title: All the Children Were Sent Away

characters: Little Red Hen — small, tough, wary
along-came-a-dog.summary: A lonely stray dog finds a home on a farm and takes it upon himself to protect a small red hen from a hungry hawk. It's a tender story of devotion between unlikely friends.
along-came-a-dog.title: Along Came a Dog

alpha-centauri.summary: A girl named Alpha Centauri sets out on a journey of discovery in a fantasy world. Details recalled lightly.
alpha-centauri.title: Alpha Centauri

amos-fortune-free-man.summary: Born an African prince, Amos Fortune is captured and enslaved in Massachusetts, and eventually buys his freedom. He settles in New Hampshire and helps others to freedom.
amos-fortune-free-man.title: Amos Fortune, Free Man

amy-and-the-sorrel-summer.summary: A children's story about a girl and a sorrel horse over a summer. Details could not be confirmed.
amy-and-the-sorrel-summer.title: Amy and the Sorrel Summer

an-american-ghost.summary: A ghost story set in America.
an-american-ghost.title: An American Ghost

anastasia-again.summary: The Krupniks move from Cambridge to the suburbs, and Anastasia hates it at first. She sets out to make the best of her new home.
anastasia-again.title: Anastasia Again!

anastasia-krupnik.summary: Ten-year-old Anastasia keeps lists of what she loves and hates, and struggles with a big change: her parents are expecting a baby. Funny and honest about growing up.
anastasia-krupnik.title: Anastasia Krupnik

and-now-miguel.summary: Miguel, a New Mexico sheepherder's son, wants to go with the men to the Sangre de Cristo mountains. He must learn what that means.
and-now-miguel.title: ...And Now Miguel

anna-to-the-infinite-power.summary: Anna is a gifted girl who discovers she has been cloned. She meets her duplicates and faces questions about identity.
anna-to-the-infinite-power.title: Anna to the Infinite Power

another-heaven-another-earth.summary: A group of colonists on a distant planet face a harsh new world and their own beliefs. The story is a thoughtful tale of survival.
another-heaven-another-earth.title: Another Heaven, Another Earth

apricots-at-midnight.summary: A girl visits a grandmother's house and finds stories among attic treasures.
apricots-at-midnight.title: Apricots at Midnight

characters: April Raintree — light-skinned, wants to pass
Cheryl Raintree — proud of her heritage
april-raintree.note: Notebook title shortened; a shortened edition was released as April Raintree (1984).
april-raintree.summary: Two Metis sisters separated in foster care grow into very different women. It is about identity and prejudice.
april-raintree.title: In Search of April Raintree

ask-me-no-questions.summary: A children's story set in Victorian England.
ask-me-no-questions.title: Ask Me No Questions

at-the-mouth-of-the-luckiest-river.summary: An Alaska Native legend retold for children.
at-the-mouth-of-the-luckiest-river.title: At the Mouth of the Luckiest River

away-goes-sally.summary: Sally and her family travel by a house on runners from Massachusetts to Maine in 1800s. Gentle first book of a series.
away-goes-sally.title: Away Goes Sally

babe-the-gallant-pig.note: Published in UK as The Sheep-Pig
babe-the-gallant-pig.summary: A runt piglet adopted by a sheepdog learns to herd sheep with kindness. Farmer Hogget is astonished.
babe-the-gallant-pig.title: Babe: The Gallant Pig

beauty-a-retelling-of-the-story-of-beaut.summary: A bookish girl nicknamed Beauty goes to live in the Beast's enchanted castle to save her father. A slow friendship grows between her and her captor.
beauty-a-retelling-of-the-story-of-beaut.title: Beauty: A Retelling of the Story of Beauty and the Beast

beezus-and-ramona.summary: Beatrice, nicknamed Beezus, finds her wildly imaginative little sister Ramona a trial, from library mishaps to a birthday party. It is a funny, honest look at sisterly frustration and love.
beezus-and-ramona.title: Beezus and Ramona

better-known-as-johnny-appleseed.summary: The life of John Chapman, who planted orchards across the early American frontier, told with warmth. He is remembered for his kindness to all living things.
better-known-as-johnny-appleseed.title: Better Known as Johnny Appleseed

black-beauty.summary: A horse tells his life story, from kind masters to cruel ones, in a plea for compassion toward animals.
black-beauty.title: Black Beauty

black-gold.summary: The true story of Black Gold, a racehorse who became a champion and won the Kentucky Derby. Henry traces his rise from an Oklahoma farm to racing glory.
black-gold.title: Black Gold

black-hearts-in-battersea.summary: Simon travels to London to study painting and finds a plot against the Duke of Battersea. With the help of the streetwise Dido Twite he chases through rooftops and rivers.
black-hearts-in-battersea.title: Black Hearts in Battersea

black-suits-from-outer-space.summary: A group of kids discover alien beings who are not what they seem. They try to warn others and put a stop to the invasion.
black-suits-from-outer-space.title: Black Suits from Outer Space

bleak-house.summary: A never-ending lawsuit entangles many lives in Victorian London. Orphan Esther Summerson, her guardian and a web of secrets are drawn together.
bleak-house.title: Bleak House

characters: Stepmother and half-brother — uneasy new family
blue-heron.summary: Maggie spends a summer with her father and his new family on the Maine coast, feeling out of place. A blue heron and a hard family moment help her find her place.
blue-heron.title: Blue Heron

blue-willow.summary: Janey is the daughter of migrant workers during the Great Depression. She hopes to hold on to a blue willow plate and find a permanent home.
blue-willow.title: Blue Willow

boy-tales-of-childhood.setting: Wales, England and Norway, 1916 to the 1930s
boy-tales-of-childhood.summary: Roald Dahl's memoir of his early years, from family holidays in Norway to miserable boarding schools. It shows the events that later turned up in his stories.
boy-tales-of-childhood.title: Boy: Tales of Childhood

bridge-to-terabithia.summary: Jess and Leslie create an imaginary kingdom in the woods. Their friendship shapes the way Jess sees the world, in a story about imagination and grief.
bridge-to-terabithia.title: Bridge to Terabithia

brighty-of-the-grand-canyon.summary: Brighty, a wild burro, roams the Grand Canyon and befriends prospector Old Timer. Based on a real burro, he helps protect a friend from a thief.
brighty-of-the-grand-canyon.title: Brighty of the Grand Canyon
